I'll work through both draft chapters systematically, applying each test.

---

**Ch 137 draft — candidate checks**

1. *"The Parsee!" cried Stubb—"he must have been caught in——"* — In the source this line is present; in the draft it is cut. The draft goes directly from "the Parsee was not there" to Stubb's follow-up line ("Aye, sir… caught among the tangles of your line"). The follow-up is a *second* speech by Stubb, supplying detail after the exclamatory first cry. In the draft Stubb's detail-giving line still parses on its own. No structural break — just compression.

2. *"Let me first help thee towards the bulwarks, sir."* — Cut in the draft; the carpenter's comment about the ferrule is also cut. The dialogue around the leg is compressed but nothing left in the draft is orphaned.

3. Starbuck's speech: *"thy evil shadow gone"* — "evil shadow" = Fedallah/the Parsee. The draft has established the Parsee's disappearance just above. A reader without the source can infer "evil shadow" = the Parsee. Not a finding.

4. Starbuck's line: *"ever since that hour we both saw—thou know'st what, in one another's eyes"* — The source keeps this; draft also keeps it. The referent ("what they both saw") is deliberately vague even in the source; not a coherence break introduced by compression.

5. Ahab mutters: *"The things called omens! Oh! how valiantly I seek to drive out of others' hearts what's clinched so fast in mine!"* — In the source Ahab prefaces this with "And yesterday I talked the same to Starbuck there, concerning my broken boat." The draft cuts that preamble but the mutter still parses. Not a finding.

6. The carpenter's ferrule remark is an authorized-cut residue (minor character compression of the carpenter's line). The draft omits *"The ferrule has not stood, sir," said the carpenter* but nothing in the surviving draft refers back to it. No orphan.

7. *"As with Fedallah the day before, so Ahab was now found grimly clinging to his boat's broken half"* — this line is in the *source* but CUT from the draft. The draft just says "Ahab was found grimly clinging to his boat's broken half." No orphan created.

Ch 137 draft appears structurally clean.

---

**Ch 138 draft — candidate checks**

**Candidate 1 — "the voice from the cabin-window"**

Source: *"The sharks! the sharks!" cried a voice from the low cabin-window there; "O master, my master, come back!"* — present in the draft verbatim. No issue.

**Candidate 2 — Starbuck's truncated soliloquy**

Draft: *"Oh! my God! what is this that shoots through me, and leaves me so deadly calm, yet expectant!"*

In the source this is followed by a long continuation: *"Future things swim before me…Mary, girl!…Mast-head there!…drive off that hawk! see! he pecks—he tears the vane"—pointing to the red flag flying at the main-truck—"Ha! he soars away with it!—Where's the old man now?"* 

The hawk tearing the vane/flag from the main-truck is established here in the source. That detail becomes narratively load-bearing in the final scene (Tashtego nailing the flag back, the sky-hawk caught under the hammer). The draft cuts the flag/hawk episode from Starbuck's soliloquy but Ahab's order to nail a flag aloft is retained in the draft: *"marking the main-truck bare, Ahab shouted for a fresh flag and hammer to be nailed aloft."* So the flag's absence from the truck IS established in the draft, though via a different path. A reader can follow the chain. Not a finding.

**Candidate 3 — Ahab's mast-head speech and the Parsee's prophecy**

Draft: *"What's that he said? he should still go before me, my pilot; and yet to be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea? Aye, like many more, thou told'st direful truth as touching thyself, O Parsee; but, Ahab, there thy shot fell short."*

"He" and "my pilot" — referent is the Parsee. In the preceding draft chapter (Ch 137 draft), Ahab says: *"he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish—How's that?"* So the Parsee-as-pilot and the prophecy about being "seen again" are established in Ch 137 draft. Now in Ch 138 draft, the Parsee's body HAS been seen (lashed to the whale's back). A competent reader, having read both draft chapters, can parse "thou told'st direful truth as touching thyself, O Parsee" — but "there thy shot fell short" is more opaque.

In the source Ch 137, Ahab's mutter establishes the riddle: *"he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish."* In Ch 138 source, Ahab's mast-head speech unpacks it: *"he should still go before me, my pilot; and yet to be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea, supposing I descend those endless stairs? and all night I've been sailing from him, wherever he did sink to."* Both versions (source and draft) retain this. The Parsee's body has now been found lashed to the whale, so "thou told'st direful truth" parses. "There thy shot fell short" means Ahab cannot yet see what "second hearse" means — this is clarified two paragraphs later when the ship is called "the second hearse." A reader can follow this. Not a finding.

**Candidate 4 — "Befooled, befooled!" and the hearse prophecy**

Draft: *"Befooled, befooled!—Aye, Parsee! I see thee again.—Aye, and thou goest before; and this, this then is the hearse that thou didst promise."*

What is "the hearse"? The Parsee's prophecy about a hearse was established in an earlier chapter. Has the draft established it? This requires a check of whether the hearse prophecy was established in preceding draft chapters. The prophecy ("thou shalt see two hearses") would be from Ch 117 source territory — but Ch 117 is on the authorized digression-removal list ("Ch 117 — Sea as gilder; quiet interlude in the boats"). However, the hearse prophecy is not a digression — in the source it is delivered during a gam-like quiet scene. Let me check: Ch 117 source title is "The Whale Watch" — Fedallah delivers his prophecy to Ahab in that chapter. It IS on the authorized removal list ("Ch 117 — Sea as gilder; quiet interlude in the boats").

If Ch 117 was cut, was the prophecy picked up elsewhere? In the Ch 137 draft, Starbuck says *"thy evil shadow gone"* but does not spell out the prophecy. In Ch 137 draft Ahab mutters: *"he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish—How's that?—There's a riddle now might baffle all the lawyers…"* This establishes that *some* prophecy exists (that the Parsee would go before AND be seen again), but the hearse element is not stated.

Now in Ch 138 draft Ahab says *"this, this then is the hearse that thou didst promise."* A reader of the draft who has not read the source has no prior mention of any hearse promise. The word "hearse" appears without a definitional or referential gloss. The prophecy is the entire basis for Ahab's exclamation and for "The ship! The hearse!—the second hearse!" fifty lines later. Without knowing what was promised, the reader cannot understand why Ahab is interpreting the Parsee's body on the whale's back as a "hearse," or why the ship's sinking becomes the "second hearse."

This is a **missing definitional gloss** (Test 4) and also a **dangling demonstrative** — "the hearse that thou didst promise" — "the hearse" has no antecedent in any preceding draft passage.

I need to check whether this is a direct residue of the *authorized* cut of Ch 117. It is: Ch 117's removal directly causes the missing hearse prophecy. Per the instructions: *"Dangling references… that are direct residues of these authorized cuts… are EXPECTED and NOT findings."* 

So this is an authorized-cut residue. NOT a finding.

**Candidate 5 — "The ship! The hearse!—the second hearse!" cried Ahab**

For the same reason — authorized residue of Ch 117 cut. NOT a finding.

**Candidate 6 — the voice from the cabin-window**

Source: the voice crying "O master, my master, come back!" is Pip's (implied by context in the source — a voice from below). In the draft the voice is unattributed. But in the source too the voice is anonymous ("a voice from the low cabin-window"). Pip is an authorized-surviving character (not on the removal list) but is not named here even in the source. No proper-name issue. Not a finding.

**Candidate 7 — "While Daggoo and Queequeg were stopping the strained planks" → draft: "As Daggoo and Queequeg stopped the strained planks"**

Both names survive in the draft. Both are established major/recurring characters (harpooneers, present throughout the novel). Not minor unglossed names.

**Candidate 8 — the broken-pivot in Starbuck's appeal**

Source Starbuck: *"never, never wilt thou capture him, old man—In Jesus' name no more of this, that's worse than devil's madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; thy very leg once more snatched from under thee; thy evil shadow gone—all good angels mobbing thee with warnings:—what more wouldst thou have?—Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world? Oh, oh,—Impiety and blasphemy to hunt him more!"*

Ch 137 draft version: *"never, never wilt thou capture him, old man—In Jesus' name no more of this, that's worse than devil's madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; thy very leg once more snatched from under thee; thy evil shadow gone—all good angels mobbing thee with warnings:—what more wouldst thou have? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Oh, oh,—Impiety and blasphemy to hunt him more!"*

The source has three rhetorical questions; the draft cuts the first ("Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man?") and the third ("Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world?"). What remains ("Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea?") still parses. Not a broken pivot — just compressed rhetoric.

**Candidate 9 — Ahab's response to Starbuck re: "ever since that hour we both saw"**

Draft Ch 138: *"Starbuck, of late I've felt strangely moved to thee."* — source includes *"ever since that hour we both saw—thou know'st what, in one another's eyes."* The draft cuts this clause. The remaining sentence parses and still conveys the meaning (Ahab's unusual tenderness toward Starbuck). This is merely less-ornamented. Not a finding.

**Candidate 10 — "Aye, and thou goest before; and this, this then is the hearse that thou didst promise. But I hold thee to the last letter of thy word. Where is the second hearse?"**

Already assessed under Candidate 4 — authorized cut residue.

**Candidate 11 — Tashtego nailing the flag**

Draft: *"marking the main-truck bare, Ahab shouted for a fresh flag and hammer to be nailed aloft."* Then later: *"Tashtego's mast-head hammer hung suspended; the red flag half wrapped him as with a plaid."* 

In the source, Starbuck's long soliloquy explicitly mentions the hawk tearing the flag away (*"he tears the vane…he soars away with it!"*), which explains why the mast-head is bare and a new flag must be nailed. In the draft Starbuck's soliloquy is cut short before that passage, but the draft supplies the explanation via Ahab's order (*"marking the main-truck bare, Ahab shouted for a fresh flag and hammer to be nailed aloft"*). This establishes why the flag needs nailing. Tashtego's action with the hammer is thus properly set up. Not a finding.

**Candidate 12 — "the submerged savage beneath"**

Draft: *"the submerged savage beneath, in his death-gasp, kept his hammer frozen there"* — "the submerged savage" = Tashtego. Tashtego has been named and placed at the mast-head in the immediately preceding draft paragraphs. The descriptor is clear and the reader can follow it. Not a finding.

**Candidate 13 — "the Indian at the mainmast"**

Draft: *"But as the last whelmings poured over the sunken head of the Indian at the mainmast"* — "the Indian" = Tashtego, who has been repeatedly named in the immediately preceding paragraphs of the draft. Clear by context. Not a finding.

---

After exhaustive checking, all apparent seams in the Ch 138 draft that involve missing prophecy material (the Parsee's hearse promise) are direct residues of the authorized cut of Ch 117, and are therefore explicitly excluded from findings per the instructions. No other sentence in either draft chapter fails any of the seven structural tests in a way that would genuinely confuse a competent reader.
